It's interesting to consider how much is involved when you press that 'submit reply' button. All the data you're sending is wrapped up in a special way. And then sent to routers and other forms of infrastructure along all sorts of mediums. And then it gets to Voat who is able to 'unwrap' the package and handle its contents before sending off some more packets to you. Sometimes packets get dropped. Sometimes packets even arrive out of order due to handling speed. But from our perspective, it just works.

Imagine, as a human, if you could do this with any other driver within a reasonable distance of yourself. And we also had the ability to process things on the order of millionths of a second. With autonomous vehicles things like stop signs, red lights, and traffic laws as a whole will become antiquated. Vehicles will need to be able to communicate for very atypical behavior for dealing with things like structural damage, disabled vehicles, inclement weather, etc. And when things are flowing well, our current traffic systems designed for humans would function as little more than a bottle neck. Kind of like when you're a red light with nobody around, yet the law doesn't allow you to run it - because humans are not trusted to have the correct judgement there.

So in theory yes. In practice? I hope not. This is a good display of driving skill, even if he misjudges the turn the first time. But it's also a maneuver that blocks an entire 4-way intersection for more than a minute. I'd hope there was a logistical mistake that left him in that situation. Perhaps he shaved a few miles off his journey by going through the residential area rather than going a less direct - but less 'intricate' path. For a human who can't drive more than 11 hours a day - every mile and minute matters. For an AI that's driving near 24 hours a day (and literally 24 hours once we start implementing infrastructure for wireless recharging) safety and minimizing risk become the most valuable players.

There will even be changing economics. Drivers are relatively expensive. To optimize profit companies are obligated to load trucks as much as they possibly can. Electric vehicles change the equation with a $0 driver cost. And fleet driving may even make multiple smaller trucks more efficient than just one large one due to a wind breaker in the front. So this video, to me, also brings up another question. Not only could an AI make this turn, but should it be in a situation where it has to make that turn?
